Paired messages let historians see what he thought could not wait and what he wanted answered together. For readers, this second text completes a day's diplomacy between the two leaders, three months before the Normandy landings, when every week carried decisions that could not be recalled.

Two Pearson messages in four days mark quickening Canadian arrangements. The conference was fast approaching by then. Quebec City would host Roosevelt and Churchill. Both leaders brought large staffs with them. Canada's diplomats smoothed the way from both capitals. For readers, the message underlines a summit's hidden labor. Host country envoys supplied that labor capably in 1944. Their work rarely reached the headlines.
frus-1944-quebec-d155:

The first would attach a French military mission under General Blaizot to Southeast Asia Command headquarters. The second would establish in India a Corps Léger d'Intervention, apparently already formed at Algiers. Hull warned that although the suggestions looked military, they carried wide political implications. For that reason, he wrote, they were referred to Roosevelt for decision rather than settled by the department.
frus-1944-quebec-d255:

The message, Facs 78, was drafted at the 172d meeting, where Brooke had argued Eisenhower understressed the northern approach and the ports. Both points went into the text.

First, the chiefs drew Eisenhower's attention to the advantages of the northern line of approach into Germany over the southern, noting with satisfaction that he appeared of the same mind. Second, they stressed the necessity of opening the northwest ports, particularly Antwerp and Rotterdam, before bad weather set in. Approval, in other words, came with a clear statement of allied priorities.

Human evolution, in her telling, is spiritual first and physical second.

Lost lands and giant early races fill the narrative, drawn from her reading of myth, geology, and Eastern scripture. Sayings of Confucius, gathered by his students, fill the Analects, the most quoted book in Chinese history. James Legge translated them from his Chinese Classics series into a standalone English volume. Confucius lived in troubled times and taught rulers and pupils how to live rightly.

Legge's Victorian English is formal, but the Master's voice comes through: dry, warm, and practical. For over two thousand years, students in China learned these lines by heart.

Newbell Niles Puckett, a sociologist, gathered Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro from fieldwork across the South, and his 1926 book became a classic of American folklore. Hoodoo, haints, conjure, and rootwork fill its chapters, reported from the people who practiced and feared them.

The Liezi is one of the classic books of Taoism, named for the sage Lieh Tzu, said to have lived in the fourth century BC. Its chapters mix fable, dialogue, and wonder tales. Chinese tradition ranks it beside the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi.

Beneath the humor sits a steady teaching: let things take their course, hold life lightly, and distrust the busy mind's alarms.
inigo-jones-stone-heng-restored-1655:
Architect Inigo Jones surveyed Stonehenge for King James and gave his verdict in Stone-Heng Restored. The book appeared in 1655, after Jones's death. Jones had reshaped English building with classical design.

He argues the stones are a Roman temple, built to a sky god. His drawings impose neat geometry on the rough circle. The theory is wrong, as later work has shown. Yet the survey counts as a pioneering act of field study. Jones treated the ruin as architecture to measure, not magic to fear, and that shift mattered. Bold error can still move a field forward.
capron-modern-spiritualism-1855:
E. W. Capron told the first tale of the Fox girls in Modern Spiritualism, his book of 1855. Capron was a news man who knew the kin at first hand. Two girls in a farm house heard raps that seemed to spell words. Crowds came, press took it up, and a faith was born in a span of months.

Capron prints the facts as he saw them, plus the wild zeal they sparked. His sub name grants both: facts and fanatic zeal. The book is the first full past of the faith. All tales since start with his pages.
wathen-the-golden-colony-1855:
George Henry Wathen tours a gold mad land in The Golden Colony, his book of 1855. Wathen, a sage of stones, went to Victoria in its gold rush prime. He tells of mines, towns, roads, and the wild new wealth of the place. His eye is keen for both rock and man in a land turned upside down by greed and hope.

Midst the tour stands a rare scrap: a turf out line of a bunyip, cut in the soil at Challicum in late 1854. Wathen gauged it on site. That note is a key source on the beast.
agrippa-fourth-book-occult-philosophy-16:
Robert Turner puts a pack of rite texts in English in the Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy set, out in London in 1655. The lead text bears Agrippa's name, though sages doubt he writ it. It teaches how to call and bind souls by name, hour, and rite. With it stand Agrippa's Geomancy, the craft of fate by earth marks, and two more famed texts of the art.

Peter de Abano's craft and the Arbatel, a book of bright souls, fill the set. Turner gave English mages their chief store of rite. The book is a grimoire shelf in one.
black-experiments-magnesia-alba-1755:
Joseph Black, a Scots doctor and chemist, read these trials to a learned group in Edinburgh in 1755. His test stuff was magnesia alba, a white earth used in drugs of the day. He also worked on quicklime and other such stuffs.

By weight and heat, Black showed that these stuffs hold a gas he named fixed air. That gas is what we now call carbon dioxide, though he had no such name for it. His strict use of the scales set a new bar and shook the old phlogiston scheme.
hare-experimental-investigation-spirit-m:
Robert Hare was a US chemist of note who built lab gear. His Experimental Investigation of the Spirit Manifestations came out in 1855. Hare had set out to mock the spirit craze of his day. His tests with his own gear, the spiritoscope, turned his mind round.

The gear was made to bar fraud: the medium could not touch the dial. Yet the dial moved, Hare says, and spelled out words of sense. He came out in print as a convert to the new creed. The book is the first of its kind to bring lab craft to the seance.
whitman-leaves-of-grass-1855:
Walt Whitman published Leaves of Grass in Brooklyn in 1855, at his own cost. The slim first edition held twelve untitled poems and a bold prose preface. Whitman set the type himself and sent free copies to famed writers of the day.

The long lead poem, later called Song of Myself, praises body and soul alike. Whitman hails grass, labor, cities, and the vast American scene around him. His free verse broke the rules of meter that ruled his age's verse. Emerson praised the book while most critics scorned or ignored its new voice. All later editions of Whitman's life work grew from this seed.
trollope-warden-1855:
Anthony Trollope published The Warden in 1855, the gentle opening of his Barchester novels of cathedral life. The tale turns on Mr. Harding's conscience over his cathedral sinecure at Hiram's Hospital in Barchester town. Trollope, a post office surveyor, found his true subject in the clergy and county society of Barsetshire here.

Harding, a kind old clergyman, holds a rich wardenship over twelve bedesmen with a tiny true workload. A young reformer, John Bold, charges in the press that the charity's funds are being misused by the church. Archdeacon Grantly urges fight, but Harding's conscience will not let him keep a post under public doubt. He resigns, the suit collapses, and the hospital stands empty in one of Trollope's saddest quiet closes in fiction. The small scale hides the moral care that made Barchester a world readers revisit.
kant-critique-pure-reason-meiklejohn-185:
Immanuel Kant first published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781, the founding work of his philosophy. The English text here is J. M. D. Meiklejohn's translation of 1855. Kant asks what human reason can know and where its limits lie. He argues the mind shapes experience through forms like space, time, and cause.

Kant distinguishes what appears to us from things as they are in themselves. He tests reason's claims about God, the soul, and the world as a whole. The book set the terms for later thought about knowledge and metaphysics. It is famously hard to read. Few works of philosophy have had a deeper or longer influence.
macaulay-history-england-vol-3-1855:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 3 of his History of England in 1855. This volume covers the first years of William and Mary after the Glorious Revolution of 1688. War with France, the siege of Londonderry, and the Battle of the Boyne fill the narrative. Scotland and Ireland receive long, vivid treatment.

Macaulay presents 1688 as the founding moment of English liberty and progress. His Whig faith shapes every judgment. The volume was left part of an unfinished work at his death. Even so, its sweep and detail set a standard for narrative history. Readers still enjoy Macaulay's confidence and color, even when they question his conclusions.
arbatel-of-magick-turner-1655:
Robert Turner's 1655 English translation made the Arbatel of Magick open to English readers for the first time. The Arbatel, whose Latin title means On the Magic of the Ancients, is a Renaissance handbook of spiritual wisdom. Its author is unknown, and its tone is prayerful rather than dark.

The book teaches the Olympic spirits, planetary powers said to govern the ages of the world in long turns. Its short aphorisms join magic to humility, charity, and trust in God, warning the reader against greed and pride. Protestant readers prized the Arbatel as godly magic, and it shaped English occult practice for centuries.
ady-candle-in-the-dark-1655:
Thomas Ady's Candle in the Dark, published in 1655, is a direct attack on the witch-hunters of his day. Ady was a physician in Kent who had watched trials rest on dreams, spite, and forced confessions. His title promises a small light against a great darkness of error.

He argues that witchcraft prosecutions rest on false testimony and melancholy, the sickness of mind his age mistook for sorcery. Scripture, rightly read, gives no warrant, he says, for hanging old women on such evidence. Ady's lonely protest helped prepare the later English turn against the witch trials.
macaulay-history-england-vol-4-1855:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 4 of his History of England from the Accession of James II in 1855. Macaulay, a famed essayist and politician, set out to tell England's story from 1685 onward. His history sold hugely and read like a novel.

William III's reign fills this volume, with war in Ireland and Europe, plots at home, and battles over money and power. Macaulay praised the settlement of 1688 and the growth of liberty, and he judged its enemies harshly. His confident Whig view shaped how Victorians saw their past. The volume shows his gifts at full stretch: clear narrative, vivid scenes, and strong opinions on every page.
faraday-experimental-researches-vol3-185:
Volume 3 of Faraday's Experimental Researches in Electricity appeared in 1855, holding Series 20 through 30. Michael Faraday's later series turned to magnetism's action on light and to the magnetic character of all matter. The volume completes the great run of his electrical papers.

Faraday showed that a magnetic field rotates the plane of polarized light, the first proof that light and magnetism are linked. He sorted materials into magnetic and diamagnetic kinds and mapped fields with iron filings. His lines of force, once doubted, here stand as a full way of picturing electric action. Maxwell built his equations on this ground. The volume closes a founding work of physics.
vesalius-de-humani-corporis-fabrica-1555:
Andreas Vesalius was a Flemish doctor who studied the human body by cutting open corpses himself, not just by reading old books. His great anatomy work first appeared in 1543. This Latin text is his own revised second edition, published in 1555. No public-domain English translation exists, so the work is presented here in Latin.

Inside, Vesalius describes bones, muscles, nerves, and organs in careful order, correcting many errors copied from Galen for over a thousand years. Detailed woodcut pictures showed the body layer by layer. The book founded modern anatomy because it trusted direct observation over ancient authority. Doctors and artists studied it for centuries.
browning-men-and-women-1855:
Robert Browning was an English poet who made his fame with dramatic monologues, poems spoken by a single character. Men and Women, published in 1855, collects fifty-one of them. It was the book that finally won him a wide audience.

Each poem lets a speaker reveal himself while telling a story. Readers meet Renaissance painters, scheming dukes, lovers, and monks. Famous pieces include Fra Lippo Lippi and Andrea del Sarto, both about art and ambition. Because the speakers expose their own motives, the poems feel like short plays. The collection is Browning's breakthrough work, the one that fixed his place among the major Victorian poets.
longfellow-hiawatha-1855:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published The Song of Hiawatha in 1855, and it sold faster than almost any poem of the century. Longfellow built his hero from Ojibwe legends gathered by the ethnographer Henry Schoolcraft, blended with a Finnish epic's driving meter. The result became America's most-read long poem.

Hiawatha, a culture hero of the lake country, grows from a miraculous childhood to manhood among the Ojibwe. He fasts, wrestles the corn spirit, builds a birch canoe, and woos Minnehaha of the Dakotas. Their wedding feast, her death in a famine winter, and his final departure west fill the closing cantos. The trochaic rhythm is unmistakable and endlessly parodied. For better and worse, the poem fixed the national myth of the noble savage.
nerval-aurelia-french-1855:
Gérard de Nerval wrote Aurélia in the last months of his life, and it appeared in 1855, the year he died. The text here is the French original. Nerval called it a descent into dream, an account of his own mental illness and the visions that came with it.

In Aurélia a lost love merges with figures of myth and faith. Dreams open doors between the living, the dead, and the divine. Nerval moves between lucid reflection and wild, haunted imagery. Later French writers, above all the surrealists, prized the book as a map of the dreaming mind. It stands beside his tale Sylvie as his most loved prose work.
commynes-memoirs-scoble-vol-1-1855:
Philippe de Commynes served Charles the Bold of Burgundy, then crossed to Louis XI of France and became his trusted adviser. His Memoirs, the first great political memoir of the modern kind, tell what he saw at both courts. Andrew Scoble translated the work, and this first volume, from 1855, holds books one through five.

Commynes watches the wars of Burgundy and France, the cunning of Louis, and the pride that ruins Charles at Nancy. He draws lessons on power with a cool, worldly hand: keep faith, buy peace cheap, fear your own anger. Kings read him for centuries as a handbook of rule. His voice, plain and knowing, still sounds modern.
commynes-memoirs-scoble-vol-2-1855:
The second volume of Andrew Scoble's Commynes, from 1855, holds books six through eight of the Memoirs. It adds the Scandalous Chronicle of Jean de Troyes, a Paris record of the same years. Commynes here follows the French court past the death of Louis XI into the reign of Charles VIII.

The young king invades Italy in 1494, and Commynes, sent as envoy, watches the old Italian order crack. He judges popes, dukes, and his own master with the same calm eye. Jean de Troyes adds the street view of Paris under Louis, its feasts, crimes, and court scandals. Together the two texts close the great memoir of the age. Commynes remains the first modern voice in political writing.
alan-of-lille-de-fide-catholica-1855:
Alan of Lille was the universal doctor of the twelfth-century schools. He wrote De Fide Catholica contra Haereticos, On the Catholic Faith Against the Heretics, in four books around 1200. The text here is drawn from the Migne Patrologia Latina, volume 210, in its 1855 reprint, and it is in Latin. Alan aimed his book at the Cathars, the Waldensians, the Jews, and the Muslims in turn.

He tries a bold method: to argue from reason and from texts his foes accept, since they scorn his own authorities. The work is the first systematic anti-heretical summa of the schools. Alan's wide reading fills it with authorities marshaled like troops. It shows the classroom arming itself for the age of the Inquisition.
snow-cholera-1855:
John Snow argued in On the Mode of Communication of Cholera that the disease travels through fouled water. The second edition of 1855 is the famous one. Snow mapped deaths around the Broad Street pump in London's Soho. The cluster of cases pointed at the pump's water like a finger.

He traces outbreaks to sewage leaking into wells and rivers. His evidence joins maps, case counts, and door to door inquiry. The book founded epidemiology, the science of tracking disease in populations. Germ theory later confirmed what his method had shown. The Gutenberg text keeps his tables and reasoning clear. Public health still teaches his pump story.
zoist-vol-13-1855:
Volume thirteen of The Zoist, from April 1855 to January 1856, completes the journal's run. Elliotson founded the journal in 1843 and edited all thirteen volumes. Mesmerism and cerebral physiology shared its pages to the end. The final volume carries the usual reports of trance, cure, and somnambulist sight.

With it closes the most important English journal the mesmeric movement ever had. Surgical cases, debates, and wonders stand preserved across the whole set. The mesmerism to hypnotism debate found its archive here. Later ages dismissed much of it, yet the record endures. Readers can now follow the cause from first trumpet to last. Few movements documented themselves so fully.
douglass-my-bondage-1855:
My Bondage and My Freedom, from 1855, is Frederick Douglass's second and fuller autobiography. By then he was a famed speaker, editor, and leader, legally free after British friends bought his liberty. He retells his early life with ten more years of thought behind it.

The bondage half gives the fullest account of his enslavement, his masters, and his escape. The freedom half traces his rise as an orator and his break with the Garrisonians. Douglass writes with open anger and sharp analysis of slavery as a system. Many readers judge it his greatest book. An introduction by James McCune Smith frames the enlarged edition.
fielding-voyage-lisbon-1755:
Fielding's Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon appeared in 1755, months after his death. Dying of dropsy and gout, he had sailed for Portugal in 1754 seeking health, as his doctors advised. He kept a journal of the slow, painful crossing.

Storms, calms, bad food, and a bullying captain fill the record, told with wit that pain could not kill. Fielding also argues for reforms in how England fed and shipped its sailors. His farewell preface, knowing he would not return, is among his most moving pages. The little book closes the career of the novelist who founded a form and served as London's magistrate.
plos-pone-0003455:

The team traced that failure to a broken regulator in the germ. With the regulator off, the germ switched on several virulence factors at once. That combined attack left neutrophils unable to control the infection. The study shows how one control fault can arm a common germ. That burst of weapons helps explain the speed of the worst invasive cases.
plos-pone-0003555:
Tomokazu Konishi and co-authors compared gene chip platforms in this 2008 methods paper. Microarrays read the activity of thousands of genes at once. Several rival platforms of chips compete in labs. Results from unlike platforms were often doubted.

Their parametric framework yielded matching results on two platforms. The same data gave coincident gene lists under that analysis. Biological truth can survive a switch of machines, given sound statistics. The work reassures labs comparing older and newer chip data. Gene chips remain a workhorse even as direct sequencing grows cheaper each year.
plos-pone-0003655:
Corinne E. Griguer, Claudia R. Oliva, Eric Gobin, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. CD133 is a protein often used to pick out supposed stem cells in glioma, a brain tumor. Glioma cells also suffer weak energy supply and low oxygen.

The team tested whether energy stress itself switches CD133 on. They found CD133 marks glioma cells under bioenergetic stress, not a fixed stem cell class. That shift in meaning matters, because it changes what researchers think they are isolating when they sort tumor cells by this protein.
plos-pone-0003755:
Maria B. Ospina, Jennifer Krebs Seida, Brenda Clark, and colleagues published this systematic review in PLOS ONE in 2008. Behavioral and developmental therapies for autism spectrum disorder are widely used and widely debated. Claims about how well they ease core symptoms vary a lot. The team set out to summarize the clinical evidence.

They gathered and weighed studies of these interventions for children with autism. The review sorts which approaches have real support and which rest on thin evidence. For families and clinicians, it separates supported care from hype in a field full of promises.
plos-pone-0003855:
Mikael Le Clech published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Centrioles are cylinders built from nine triplets of microtubules. They are needed to form centrosomes, flagella, and cilia, yet how they are built is poorly understood. Duplication of the centrosome begins as the cell readies to copy its DNA.

Le Clech studied the protein CAP350 and its place in that process. He shows CAP350 keeps centriolar tubules stable and helps centrioles assemble correctly. The finding fills in part of how these nine-triplet organizing centers get built right.
plos-pone-0003955:

Their PLOS ONE article couples two contagions, fear and disease, in one model. Each spread shapes the other's course through the population. Math and computer runs explore how the pairing changes outbreak size. Public health plans can use such models to foresee behavior-driven turns. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004055:
Emily J. Capra, Sonja M. Skrovanek, and Leonid Kruglyak compared development gene programs in two worm strains in 2008. Gene activity changes across development in C. elegans. It also varies between genetically distinct strains. Earlier time-course studies of worm development were incomplete.

Their PLOS ONE article profiles two C. elegans isolates side by side. Comparing strains shows which developmental patterns are universal or strain-specific. Such variation is raw material for evolution within a species. It also warns model-organism labs that one strain cannot speak for all. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004155:

The team studied short peptides, protein fragments, taken from integrase itself that bind a second viral protein called Rev. They report that these peptides stimulate the integration of the viral genome. Finding fragments that change how the virus inserts its DNA may point to new ways to interfere with HIV's life cycle.
plos-pone-0004255:
Marie Garnier-Lhomme and colleagues published this cell membrane study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The inside of a eukaryotic cell is in constant motion, with membranes splitting and fusing to move cargo and rebuild compartments. The nuclear envelope, the double membrane around the DNA, is one such structure, and it breaks down when cells divide.

The authors describe remnants of that envelope that persist as fluid membranes. These remnants are enriched in sterols and polyphosphoinositides, two classes of membrane lipids. Characterising what is left of the envelope helps explain how cells rebuild their nucleus after division.
plos-pone-0004355:

Working with hepatitis C core proteins derived from liver cancer, the team show these proteins shift TGF-beta responses. Instead of tumour suppression, the signal now drives epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a change that helps cancer spread. The virus thus twists a guard into an accomplice.

plos-pone-0004555: In 2009, Mutoh, Perron, and Dimitrov compared three glowing voltage sensors. Spectrally-resolved properties of three FRET-based fluorescent protein voltage sensors were measured. plos-pone-0004655: In 2009, Mendonsa, Dobrowolska, and Lin profiled key stress signals in Alzheimer's brains. Stress signal chains in Alzheimer's were charted. The fresh-look approach was tested head-on. The study helps future care design a lot. The heavy social cost is growing fast.

braid-physiology-fascination-1855:
James Braid defends his life's work in The Physiology of Fascination, from 1855, his late reply to the critics of hypnotism. Fascination, the fixed stare of man or beast, gets his close physiological study. He refines his theory of suggestion while answering skeptics point by sharp point in print.

The founder writes with the vigor of a man still fighting for his science. Cases, trials, and tart rejoinders fill the combative pages here. He insists that trance is real, lawful, and open to study. The book is key for the history of psychology's most argued method, showing its maker in his final, feisty form.
euler-institutiones-calculi-1755:
Leonhard Euler orders the differential calculus in his Institutiones calculi differentialis, in Latin from 1755. No true textbook of the subject had existed before his. Euler takes the wild new math of Newton and Leibniz and sets it in teachable order, rule by rule, for every student to follow with profit.

Generations learned analysis from these patient, lucid Latin pages afterward. Functions, rates, and curves gain clear forms under his hand. Euler produced more math than any man of his century, perhaps of any century. This book shows his most useful gift: not discovery alone, but the power to make hard things plain for those who came after.
warsaw-pact-1955:
The Soviet Union and seven Eastern European states signed the Warsaw Pact in May 1955. Its formal title was a treaty of friendship, cooperation, and mutual assistance. Moscow announced it days after West Germany joined NATO, presenting the new bloc as the East's answer to the Western alliance.

Members pledged to aid any member that came under armed attack, and they set up a joint military command under Soviet control. In practice the alliance served as Moscow's tool for holding its satellite states in line. Soviet-led forces used its framework to crush the Hungarian rising of 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968. The pact dissolved in 1991 as the Cold War ended.
hutcheson-system-moral-philosophy-vol1-1:
Hutcheson's System of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1755, eight years after his death, published by his son from the Glasgow lectures. Hutcheson had been the most beloved teacher of the Scottish Enlightenment. The System was meant as his summa, the full statement of the moral thought he had taught for years.

Volume 1 opens with human nature: the senses, the passions, and above all the moral sense by which we approve virtue. Hutcheson argues that virtue is discerned by feeling rightly trained, not by cold reason alone. His famous standard, the greatest happiness of the greatest numbers, appears here in an early form. The volume made the teacher's fame permanent and set the agenda for his student Adam Smith. It remains the foundation book of the moral-sense school.
hutcheson-system-moral-philosophy-vol2-1:
The second volume of Hutcheson's System of Moral Philosophy followed the first in 1755, completing the posthumous work. Volume 1 had grounded morals in the moral sense. Volume 2 puts that system to work on the questions of law, rights, and government.

Hutcheson treats the rights of individuals, the grounds of political authority, and the duties that come with each station in life. He defends a right of resistance when rulers destroy the ends for which government exists, a doctrine with a long afterlife in America. Property, contracts, marriage, and war all receive careful, humane treatment. The closing book turns moral thought into political thought. Readers have called the System the charter of the Scottish Enlightenment, with liberty rooted in the moral sense itself.
romanus-pontifex-1455:
Pope Nicholas V issued Romanus Pontifex in 1455, addressed to King Afonso V of Portugal. Portuguese ships were then pushing down the coast of Africa, seeking trade and a sea route east. The bull backed Portugal's claims against rival Christian powers.

The text grants Portugal rights over lands its sailors reached along and beyond the African coast. It also permits war against non-Christian peoples there and supports their capture and enslavement, language that reads brutally today. Portugal used the bull to defend its growing sea empire. The document is a key paper source for Europe's early age of expansion.

Adams prized that balance and matched Seward's firmness with a cooler tone in person. A cooler tone in person let Adams press hard points without giving offense.
frus-1861-d155:
On 10 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton as the war moved to the coasts. The letter is document 155 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

October brought the war to the coasts, with expeditions fitting out in Northern ports. Paris watched those moves for signs of Union strength. Seward's letter guided Dayton's reading of the season for the French court. A port expedition sailed for the Carolina coast late that October month. A Carolina expedition that month gave Paris fresh proof of Union reach at sea. It sailed under Du Pont and struck Port Royal in the first week of November.
frus-1861-d255:
From his post abroad, James Shepherd Pike wrote to William H. Seward on 25 September 1861. It stands as Document 255 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d55:
On 1 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 55 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d155:
Writing from London on 3 October 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent a report to Secretary of State William H. Seward, preserved as Document 155 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams served as American minister to Britain through the whole Civil War.

October opened with British debate over the American war still unsettled. A report from Adams carried his read of ministers, newspapers, and public feeling in London, the raw material for Washington's next moves. Taken with the letters around it, this dispatch helps trace how the threat of British action rose and fell that fall. Southern agents worked London's clubs and press hard, and the legation tracked their moves.
frus-1862-d255:
On 27 February 1862 William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Paris, in a report printed as Document 255 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Paris papers under that date.

Dayton's mail sailed from French ports and took about two weeks to reach Washington, so his news was seasoned by the time Seward read it. Even so, his read on the French court set the frame for American replies. This report closes the February run of the Paris file, a month of Union wins and watchful quiet from France. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d355:
A second Thouvenel instruction to Henri Mercier followed on 23 January 1862, printed as Document 355 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Edouard Thouvenel directed French foreign policy from Paris; Mercier carried it out in Washington.

Two instructions in five days suggest Paris was refining its guidance as news arrived from America and Mexico. The Atlantic lag meant such orders often answered month-old reports. Even so, the pair shows the machinery of French policy at work, and it helps explain the positions Mercier took with Seward that winter. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d455:
John Lothrop Motley, the American minister in Vienna, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 November 1861. It is Document 455 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the earliest Austrian paper in the file.

Motley had just taken up the Vienna post, and his first reports sized up an empire wary of republics and revolutions. Austria watched the American war through its own fears, yet it had little love for Britain's or France's games either. A new minister's first impressions mattered in Washington, where Seward was sorting Europe into friends, neutrals, and risks. The report opens the Austrian correspondence with a historian's eye for the forces moving under the surface.
frus-1862-d555:
Four days after his last, on 10 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. It is Document 555 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's record.

The short gap between orders reflects Sanford's habit of asking questions and Seward's habit of answering them. Brussels in 1862 was a crossroads of European gossip and intrigue, where Confederate agents also worked. A minister there needed fresh instructions often. The letter belongs to the busy spring file of the Belgian mission. In that file Washington treated a small court as a serious post. The man holding it had made it one.
frus-1862-d655:
On 15 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Robert H. Pruyn, the man picked to head the American legation in Japan. The letter is document 655 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Pruyn would take over from Townsend Harris, the first man to hold the post.

Letters to an envoy on his way out carried the charge for his mission. It told what to seek, what to avoid, and how to speak for his government. Seward's note to Pruyn is part of that hand-over. It marks the point where the Japan post passed from its founder to the men who would hold it through the war.
frus-1863p1-d55:
Christopher G. Memminger wrote this letter to Messrs. Fraser, Trenholm & Co. on 24 October 1862. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury. The firm, based in Liverpool with roots in Charleston, acted as the South's bankers in Britain. The letter is document 55 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Through Fraser, Trenholm & Co. flowed the South's money in Europe: cotton sales in, ships and arms out. A treasury letter to the firm dealt with the heart of the war's finance. This one is part of the Confederate group printed by the Union. It shows the South's cause resting, in no small part, on a Liverpool counting house.
frus-1863p1-d155:
On 13 April 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 155 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Seward's 13 April pair held its own point, in the habit of the whole file. Such splits let Adams raise each matter with the British in its own time and words. This letter closes the day's work from Washington. It belongs to the steady stream that, by the spring of 1863, had made the London brief a model of its kind.
frus-1863p1-d255:
Writing from London on 30 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 255 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d355:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 January 1863. It is document 355 of the 1863 papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons wrote as the voice of the British government in Washington. His notes carried protests, questions, and warnings that Seward had to answer with care. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d455:
Secretary William H. Seward sent an official note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 9 April 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d555:
A letter of 6 June 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 555 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d655:
From Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to Secretary William H. Seward: a letter dated 5 November 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pbio-0020055:
Jerel C. Davis and Dmitri A. Petrov examined gene copying across eukaryotic genomes in PLOS Biology in 2004. Gene duplication is a main source of new traits. When a gene is copied, one copy can keep the old job while the other is free to change.

Not all genes get copied and kept at the same rate. The authors found that proteins conserved over long spans of evolution are copied more often than others. That runs against a simple guess that the most vital genes would resist change. Their result suggests that proven, stable proteins make good raw material for new functions. It reshapes how genome scientists think about where novelty comes from.
plos-pbio-0020155:
Susan E. Ptak, Amy D. Roeder, Matthew Stephens, and their team compared a DNA hotspot in humans and chimps for PLOS Biology in 2004. Hotspots are short DNA stretches where genetic shuffling during reproduction happens far more than average. One human hotspot, called TAP2, has no match in chimpanzees.

That absence is striking, since chimps share most of our DNA. It shows hotspots can appear and vanish fast in evolution, much faster than the DNA around them. The finding changed how scientists model recombination, the shuffling that creates new gene mixes each generation. Chimp data can no longer be assumed to mirror our own hotspot map.
plos-pbio-0020355:
Ryan B. Rountree, Michael Schoor, Hao Chen, and a large team studied joint cartilage in mice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cartilage caps the ends of bones and lets joints glide. Signals through BMP receptors help build it before birth, and the team asked whether those signals still matter after birth.

They do: without BMP receptor signaling, adult cartilage breaks down and joints suffer. That means cartilage is not a set-and-forget tissue. It needs constant upkeep signals through life. The finding matters for arthritis, where cartilage loss is the core problem. A signal required for upkeep is a natural place to look for treatments that protect joints.
plos-pone-0000155:
Felix Zajitschek, John Hunt, Susanne R. K. Zajitschek, and colleagues published this cricket study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests intra-locus sexual conflict, the idea that a gene good for males can be bad for females, or the reverse. The authors measured reproductive fitness and ageing in field crickets.

As the title states, they found no such conflict over fitness or ageing in these crickets. A negative result still counts: it trims a popular theory down to the cases where evidence supports it. The study is a useful check on how widespread sexual conflict really is in wild populations.
plos-pone-0000255:
Rani E. George, Edward F. Attiyeh, Shuli Li, and colleagues published this cancer genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer of nerve tissue. The authors scan tumors genome-wide using high-density SNP arrays. These chips read hundreds of thousands of DNA markers, revealing the gains and losses that mark the cancer's genome.

Patterns of deletion and duplication point to the genes driving a tumor. A genome-wide survey gives an unbiased map of those changes in neuroblastoma. The results guide the search for outcome predictors and drug targets in a cancer that behaves very differently from child to child.
plos-pone-0000355:
Leonor Saiz and Jose M. G. Vilar published this theoretical biophysics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inside living cells, DNA loops bring distant sites together, and proteins bound on the loop change gene activity. The authors carry out a multilevel deconstruction of the in vivo behavior of these looped DNA-protein complexes, breaking their behavior down across scales.

Loops behave differently inside a crowded cell than in a test tube. A multilevel account connects molecular forces to the loop's actual dynamics in vivo. The work guides the modeling of gene regulation, where looping is a central mechanism.
plos-pone-0000455:
Irmgard Amrein and colleagues checked whether bats make new brain cells as adults, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. In many mammals, the hippocampus, a memory center, keeps producing neurons throughout life, a process called adult neurogenesis. The team examined bats, order Chiroptera, and looked for signs of that production.

They found adult neurogenesis in the bat hippocampus to be absent or at a low rate. That exception is informative: if some long-lived, big-brained mammals manage without it, the process is not a universal requirement. Comparative findings like this keep theories about why new neurons matter honest, by testing them against animals that break the pattern.
plos-pone-0000555:
Laurent Pélozuelo and colleagues studied mate choice between two forms of a crop pest moth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. European corn borers come in pheromone races: females of each race release a different scent blend, and males follow their own race's scent. The team examined assortative mating between the races, going beyond assortative meeting.

Meeting is about being in the same place; mating is about actually choosing. If the races meet but still mate within their kind, the barrier is preference, and the races may be splitting into species. Pest evolution matters practically too, since control methods often exploit the very pheromones that divide the races.
plos-pone-0000655:
Cheryl A. Stoddart, Cheryl A. Bales, Jennifer C. Bare and co-authors validated a mouse model of HIV infection in PLOS ONE in 2007. The SCID-hu Thy/Liv model implants human thymus and liver tissue in mice that lack their own immune systems. HIV-1 can then infect the human tissue. The model serves preclinical tests of antiviral drugs before human trials.

To validate it, the team used representatives of all four classes of licensed antiretrovirals. A model that answers known drugs correctly can be trusted more with unknown ones. Their endpoint analyses measured viral quantities to judge each drug. Animal models live or die by such checks.
plos-pone-0000755:
Birte Kretschmer, Katja Lüthje, Andreas H. Guse and colleagues adjusted an immune protein and watched antibody output fall, in PLOS ONE in 2007. CD83 is a membrane glycoprotein known as an important regulator of T cell maturation in the thymus and of T cell responses in the body. The team had recently reported a function on B cells too: forcing CD83 expression everywhere interfered with antibody production.

Working in vitro, they report that B cells carrying extra CD83 raise IL-10, a calming immune signal, and reduce immunoglobulin secretion. CD83 thus modulates B cell function directly. Fine control of antibody output matters in vaccination, allergy, and autoimmune disease alike.
plos-pone-0000855:
Carl Troein, Dag Ahrén, Morten Krogh and colleagues asked whether the standard way microbes control their metabolism is truly the best way. Transcriptional regulation of metabolic pathway genes is an approach that works well, nearly universal in microorganisms. The lac operon of E. coli is one example: cells make enzymes and transporters only when a nutrient is present, so cells do not waste resources.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE question is whether that strategy is optimal for fitness, or merely good and historically locked in. Such tests split what evolution perfected from what it merely settled for. The answer shapes how engineers should design synthetic microbes: copy nature, or improve on it.
plos-pone-0000955:
Kira Makarova and co-authors studied the genes behind radiation survival in a second hardy bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Deinococcus bacteria withstand radiation, UV light and drying that would kill most life. The first of the group to be fully sequenced was Deinococcus radiodurans.

Here the team analyze Deinococcus geothermalis, a heat loving relative. Their title reports that the pool of extreme resistance genes shrinks under comparison. Shared toughness across species may rest on fewer genes than single genome studies suggested. Narrowing that pool focuses the search for how these bacteria repair shattered DNA so well.
plos-pone-0001055:
Saliou Fall and colleagues argued that gene transfer rules in bacteria may be a side effect of DNA repair. They published the work in PLOS ONE in 2007. Horizontal gene transfer, genes moving between unrelated bacteria, is the major force in bacterial genome evolution. Open questions remain about which genes move, and how often.

The authors focus on genetic transformation, uptake of loose DNA from outside. They suggest its regulation rides on the machinery that repairs DNA, a spandrel, a feature that exists because of another feature. That reframing changes where to look for controls on gene swapping, a process behind antibiotic resistance spread.
plos-pone-0001155:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is among the most aggressive and deadly cancers. Marina Pasca di Magliano and co-authors examined a signaling pathway in this cancer in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The pathway is Wnt signaling, a system embryos use to organize growth, and most of these tumors also carry mutations in the Kras gene.

The authors report common activation of the canonical Wnt pathway in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. A growth pathway borrowed from development, switched on in most tumors, is a possible point of attack. The paper adds to the case that this cancer leans on embryonic programs to sustain itself.
plos-pone-0001255:
In survival analysis, researchers often ask whether the time until failure and the cause of failure are independent. Isha Dewan and Sangita Kulathinal study that testing problem when some causes of failure are missing, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Missing causes are common in practice, when a failure is recorded but not classified.

The authors base their test on the conditional probabilities of failure from a specific cause, given no failure up to a fixed time. Their method aims to stay valid even with incomplete cause data. The paper is a contribution to statistical theory for reliability and medical follow-up studies.
plos-pone-0001355:
Cre recombinase is a tool that lets researchers delete or switch genes at chosen sites in experimental animals. Controlling when it acts, however, has been inefficient. Nicolas Jullien and colleagues present a solution called DiCre, dimerizable Cre, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The concept: split Cre into two inactive halves that join only when a drug brings them together.

Conditional transgenesis using this system gives efficient temporal control over Cre activity. Timing matters because deleting a gene early in development can mask its adult role. DiCre became a widely used tool in mouse genetics after this report.
plos-pone-0001455:
Pierre Gladieux and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on apple scab, a fungus ill that hurts orchards world wide. The fungus has spread to near all apple growing lands. To predict how well control steps will work, labs must know where it came from. The team traced its spread with gene data.

Their data point to a start in Central Asia, the home of the wild apple. From there the fungus moved out with farmed apples. A clear origin tale helps growers plan for new strains. It also shows how a crop disease can ride trade and planting across the globe in a short span.
plos-pone-0001555:
Bashar Ibrahim and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that models the cell division checkpoint in a computer. This checkpoint holds a cell back until all chromosomes are locked to the split frame in the right way. Only then may the cell part its copies. Faults here seed cancer and birth ills.

Their model rebuilds the checkpoint's web of signals step by step in code. A working model lets labs test faults no bench test could reach. It also shows which links in the web matter most. Such maps help drug teams find the checkpoint's weak points in tumors.
plos-pone-0001655:
Nicholas A. Lesica and Benedikt Grothe listened in on the hearing pathway of mammals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. They asked how well the system keeps up with the timing of natural sounds, such as animal calls. Their recordings came from neurons in the inferior colliculus, a midbrain hub for hearing.

From the cells' responses to vocalization sounds, the authors derived temporal receptive fields, maps of which time patterns each cell prefers. They then judged how the pathway adjusts its timing strategy to fit natural stimuli. The full text gives the recordings, the maps, and the measures of timing accuracy. Hearing aids and speech processors copy this pathway's tricks, so knowing how it handles real-world sound timing has both basic and applied value.
plos-pone-0001755:
Sizolwenkosi Mlotshwa, Gail J. Pruss, Angela Peragine, and their co-authors studied how plants spread gene silencing in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dicer-like enzymes cut long double-stranded RNA into the small RNAs that mediate silencing. Silencing can then amplify and spread along a gene, a process called transitive silencing.

Working in Arabidopsis, the team reports that the enzyme DICER-LIKE2 plays a primary role in transitive silencing of transgenes. The full text gives the plant mutants and the silencing spread measurements. Transgene silencing is both a tool and a nuisance in plant science. It lets researchers switch genes off, but it can also shut down engineered traits that farmers want kept on.
plos-pone-0001855:
Nicaise Tuikue Ndam and co-authors analyzed gene expression of the malaria parasite in pregnancy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Malaria in pregnancy causes anemia in the mother and low birth weight. It is one of the many forms of Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Red blood cells carrying the parasite can gain sticky traits that drive how severe the malaria gets.

Their gene activity analysis shows which genes the parasite switches on in pregnancy, linked to binding in the placenta. The full text gives the gene lists and comparisons. Pregnancy malaria needs its own vaccine, and the genes specific to it are the leading vaccine parts.
plos-pone-0001955:
Connie Wong and co-authors sharpened a lab trick that turns adult cells back toward an embryo-like state, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Fusing an adult cell with a stem cell can reprogram the adult nucleus. But the process is slow, and the steps behind it were poorly known. A faster assay would let labs hunt the genes that drive the change.

The team tuned stem cell fusion to work at high efficiency, then used it as a test bed. With it, they report that a gene called Sall4 acts as an enhancer of reprogramming. Tools like this speed the search for safe ways to make patient-matched stem cells.
plos-pone-0002055:
Hugh Cahill and Jeremy Nathans promoted a simple eye reflex as a lab test for brain function in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The optokinetic reflex steadies a moving image on the retina by turning the eyes to follow it. It needs no training, can be evoked again and again, and draws on diverse brain circuits.

Those traits make it a fine quantitative test of nervous system function. The pair applied it to variation caused by genes and by drugs. A cheap behavior test that reads out deep circuitry can screen mutant mice and drug effects far faster than anatomy can.
plos-pone-0002155:
Arthur Bikbaev and co-authors studied a receptor that links learning and memory in the hippocampus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The hippocampus is a brain region vital for forming memories. A receptor called mGluR5, which senses the messenger glutamate, strongly shapes both lasting changes at synapses and learning itself.

The team blocked mGluR5 for a long period with a drug called MPEP and traced what happened next. They looked at late-phase LTP, the long-lasting strengthening of synapses tied to memory, and at how network activity changed. Their results help map the steps between one receptor and the act of learning.
plos-pone-0002255:
Rien van Haperen and co-authors tested how a fat-moving protein in blood cells affects artery disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Phospholipid transfer protein, or PLTP, rides on HDL, the so-called good cholesterol particles. In engineered mice, high PLTP lowers HDL and raises atherosclerosis, the buildup of artery plaque, and PLTP is found in human plaques too.

The team raised PLTP levels in bone marrow derived cells and watched the effect on disease. Their results show this source of PLTP alone can drive atherosclerosis. The finding sharpens the case that how fat is shuffled in blood helps decide whose arteries clog.
plos-pone-0002355:
Collin Elsea and co-authors tested whether blocking a stress signal can ease a harsh side effect of chemotherapy. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Patients on systemic chemotherapy often suffer deep fatigue like the sickness behavior that follows infection. That state is driven by inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1 beta, TNF-alpha, and IL-6, released when drugs damage tissues.

The team inhibited the p38 MAPK pathway in their models. Blocking it suppressed the cytokine surge caused by etoposide, 5-fluorouracil, and doxorubicin, without weakening the drugs' tumor-killing activity. Separating a cancer drug's benefit from its misery is a prize worth chasing for patient care.
plos-pone-0002455:
Wood-Kaczmar led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Alison Wood-Kaczmar, Sonia Gandhi, Zhi Yao, among others. Its subject is pINK1 Is Necessary for Long Term Survival and Mitochondrial Function in Human Dopaminergic Neurons. Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common age-related neurodegenerative disease.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002555:
Santos and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Nuno R. dos Santos, Maryvonne Williame, Stéphanie Gachet, among others. Its subject is relB-Dependent Stromal Cells Promote T-Cell Leukemogenesis. The Rel/NF-κB transcription factors are often activated in solid or hematological malignancies.

In most cases, NF-κB activation is found in malignant cells and results from activation of the canonical NF-κB pathway. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002655:
Janyce A. Sugui and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was genes differentially expressed in conidia and hyphae of aspergillus fumigatus upon exposure to human neutrophils. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Janyce A. Sugui, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common etiologic agent of invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002755:
Pu Zhang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was expression analysis of the NLRP gene family suggests a role in human preimplantation development. The catalog record names Pu Zhang first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The NLRP (Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain, Leucine rich Repeat and Pyrin domain containing) family, also referred to as NALP family. It goes on to note a further point. Several NLRP s have been indicated as being involved in reproduction as well. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002855:
Claire Gaillard and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a High-Sensitivity method for detection and measurement of HMGB1 protein concentration by High-Affinity binding to DNA hemicatenanes. Authorship is credited in the record to Claire Gaillard and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Protein HMGB1, an abundant nuclear non-histone protein that interacts with DNA and has an architectural function in chromatin. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002955:
Sakshi Shrivastava and Sharmila Mande searched bacterial genomes for parts of the type VI secretion system in 2008. That system, a needle-like device bacteria use to export proteins, had lately been reported in cholera and two other disease bacteria. Eighteen genes had been tied to it in Vibrio cholerae.

The authors set out to identify and characterize the system's gene parts across bacterial genomes by computer analysis. Finding the parts widely would suggest the device is a common weapon. Published in PLOS ONE, the survey helps microbiologists spot this system in new genome sequences.
plos-pone-0003055:
Helen Burgess and Louis Fogg examined full melatonin profiles in a large sample in 2008. The study's aim was to map individual differences in how much melatonin people secrete and when, using profiles not suppressed by light. Lifestyle variables were then checked for links to amount and timing.

Melatonin is the hormone that signals night to the body clock. Published in PLOS ONE, complete profiles across many people show the normal human range, which single samples cannot. Sleep medicine uses such ranges to judge delayed or advanced clocks and to time light and melatonin treatment.
plos-pone-0003155:
Nicholas P. Vyleta and Stephen M. Smith report a fast effect of caffeine on glutamate signals in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Caffeine is known to trigger calcium release inside many cell types. In neurons it acts before the synapse and can change how transmitters are released. The team used the whole-cell patch-clamp method to record currents in detail.

They found that caffeine quickly and reversibly changed the frequency of events tied to glutamate-activated currents, and the title reports fast inhibition of those currents. Readers get a precise cellular account that differs from caffeine's better known actions. It adds nuance to how a common drug affects brain signalling.
plos-pone-0003255:
Christian B. Gocke and Hongtao Yu study a chromatin repressor complex in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Marks on histones in chromatin control which genes are on. A transcriptional co-repressor complex containing LSD1, CoREST and HDAC1 represses transcription. It does so by removing histone modifications associated with transcriptional activation, thereby switching genes off.

The title reports that ZNF198 holds this LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 complex steady on chromatin through its MYM-type zinc fingers. Readers learn what holds a silencing machine in place. Drugs could target such anchors in cancers where gene silencing goes wrong. The details matter for drug work on gene silencing.
plos-pone-0003355:
Alex J. Cadotte, Thomas B. DeMarse, Ping He and colleagues measure causality in neural networks in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A major goal of neuroscience is to understand the relationship between neural structures and their function. Recording of neural activity with arrays of electrodes is a primary tool employed toward this goal. arxiv-2606-16455: Researchers often need to find hidden subgroups in data mixing continuous measurements and yes/no answers. hyreg2 is an R package that estimates latent classes on such mixed data — clustering people or samples into unobserved groups. arxiv-2606-16555: Cloud platforms orchestrate services with learned policies, but those policies need the right incentives — and evidence that they work.
